n: Paul defends his authority with rapid-fire questions. He is a true apostle: he has seen the risen Lord, and the Corinthian church itself is proof of his work.

f.w: have I not seen Jesus Christ our Lord?

f.g: Free to use his rights, like the right to be supported.

n: Others might doubt Paul, but the Corinthians can’t — their conversion is the official seal stamping his apostleship as genuine.

f.g: A stamp of authenticity, like a wax seal on a document.

n: To those who question his credentials, Paul now presents his defense.

f.g: Interrogate, cross-examine, as in a legal hearing.

n: Don’t apostles have the right to be fed and housed by those they serve?

f.g: Here, right or authority.

n: Don’t they have the right to bring a believing wife along on their travels, as Peter, the other apostles, and the Lord’s brothers did?

f.g: A believing wife (a “sister” in the faith).

n: Are Paul and Barnabas the only missionaries expected to support themselves with secular work?

f.g: Refrain from working for a living.

n: Paul uses everyday examples: soldiers are paid, vineyard planters eat grapes, shepherds drink milk from their flocks. Workers deserve to benefit from their work.

f.g: At his own expense.

n: This isn’t merely human reasoning — the law of Moses teaches the same thing.

f.g: The law of Moses in the first five books of the Old Testament.

n: Moses’ law said not to muzzle an ox while it treads out grain, so it could eat as it worked. Paul asks whether God’s concern was really only for oxen.

f.w: Thou shalt not muzzle the mouth of the ox

f.g: In the KJV, any grain, such as wheat or barley.

n: The principle applies to people: those who plow and thresh should be able to work in hope of sharing the harvest.

f.g: Beats or treads grain to separate kernels from husks.

n: If Paul planted spiritual blessings among them, is it too much to receive some material support in return?

f.g: Material, physical things like food and money.

n: Others received support from the Corinthians; Paul had even more right. Yet he refused it and endured hardship so nothing would get in the gospel’s way.

f.g: Put up with everything.

n: Priests in the temple lived from the offerings brought there. Those who served at the altar received a share of the sacrifices.
Likewise, the Lord directed that full-time preachers of the gospel be supported by it.

f.w: they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel

n: But Paul has not used this right and isn’t hinting for it now. He would rather die than lose the privilege of preaching without pay.

f.g: His grounds for honest pride — preaching free of charge.

n: Preaching itself isn’t something to boast about — Paul is under divine compulsion to do it. He would be miserable if he didn’t.

f.w: woe is unto me, if I preach not the gospel

n: If he preached by his own choice, he could expect pay. But he was commissioned — entrusted with a stewardship — so preaching is simply his duty.

f.g: Here, a stewardship or commission entrusted to him.

n: His “reward” is the satisfaction of offering the gospel free of charge, not exploiting his rights.
Though free from obligation to anyone, Paul made himself everyone’s servant to win as many as possible to Christ.
Among Jews, Paul respected Jewish customs so he could reach them — for example, by having Timothy circumcised.
Among Gentiles who didn’t keep Moses’ law, he set aside those customs — though he was always under Christ’s law.
He came alongside the spiritually fragile, too. Paul adapted his approach to every audience, without compromising the gospel, to save some.

f.g: Adapting methods, not changing doctrine.

n: Paul does all this for the gospel’s sake, so that he can share in its blessings with them.

f.g: A sharer in the gospel’s blessings.

n: Corinth hosted the famous Isthmian Games. Paul says: in a race only one wins the prize, so run to win.

f.w: So run, that ye may obtain

n: Athletes in training exercise strict self-discipline to win a wreath that withers. Christians train for a crown that never fades.

f.g: Victors at the Isthmian Games received a wreath of pine or celery that soon withered.
Self-controlled.

n: Paul runs with a clear goal and boxes with purpose — not shadowboxing or swinging wildly at air.

f.g: Punching at nothing, wasted effort.

n: He disciplines his body and keeps it under control so that, after preaching to others, he himself won’t be disqualified.

f.g: Literally “give a black eye to” — strict self-discipline.
Disqualified, rejected after testing.
